blocks.text: Predictive modeling uses data to predict future outcomes. Machine learning models analyze past data patterns. These patterns help estimate what may happen next. Predictive models are used in many fields. They support planning and decision making. Predictions are based on probability. They do not always explain reasons. Understanding causality is also important. Both concepts are used together in analysis.

blocks.title: Class Activity
blocks.text: Give examples like weather prediction. Ask students whether prediction explains the cause. Discuss the difference.

Predictive outcomes are results produced by a trained model. The model uses past data to make predictions. These outcomes estimate future values or events. Prediction accuracy depends on data quality. Good training improves predictions. For example, businesses use predictions for forecasting the market or product selling trends. Healthcare uses predictions for diagnosis. Predictions support better decisions.

Causality explains why an event happens. It shows a cause-and-effect relationship. One factor directly influences another. Causality is important in scientific studies to understand real reasons behind events. Data alone may not show causality but experiments often identify causes. Causal understanding improves decisions and avoids false assumptions.

Prediction estimates what may happen based on historical data. It focuses on forecasting outcomes, where the model uses past information to estimate future values or events. For example, a model may predict a student's final grade by analysing previous marks, attendance, and study hours. Similarly, a weather model may predict tomorrow's temperature by using past weather records. A model can make accurate predictions without necessarily understanding the underlying causes. This makes prediction useful in areas such as sales forecasting, stock trend analysis, disease risk prediction, and student performance estimation.

Causation, on the other hand, explains why something happens by identifying cause-and-effect relationships between variables. It seeks to uncover the reasons behind events and how one factor directly influences another. For example, if regular study hours directly improve exam performance, then study time may be considered a cause of better grades. Similarly, if smoking directly increases the risk of lung disease, this shows a causal relationship. Understanding causality is important for decision-making because it helps avoid false assumptions and provides deeper insight into real-world problems.
